Today: A deep low begins its migration into the region. Midlevel 
moisture is streaming inland ahead of the low bringing heavy mid 
and high level clouds along with sprinkles and light showers. 
There has been a few lightning strikes near Lewiston this morning 
where there are a few midlevel circulations noted within the 
midlevels. Would not rule out a few strikes with additional 
activity in Central WA either due to subtle circulations showing 
up in the water vapor. The air mass is very warm and dry near the 
surface. As such, any rain falling is largely evaporating but this
is leading to erratic wind gusts upwards of 15 to 20 mph. Several
of the high resolution models are indicating that a few cells 
that can drive rain to the surface could result in gusts as high 
as 40 mph. 

This band of moisture and shower activity will slowly lift south to 
north and clear across the International border early Saturday 
morning and the upper low will begin to migrate to the WA Coast, 
into the North Cascades overnight and across NE WA and N ID Sunday
morning. As the low and associated 500mb cold pool migrates 
inland, lapse rates will continue to steepen with lower levels 
remaining in the 90s. Areas of NE WA and N ID will only cool 3-4 
degrees from Friday and Heat Advisories have been extended. One of
the main concerns for Saturday will be the potential for 
thunderstorms developing. Initially, storms are expected to fire 
over the North Cascades where the upper level cooling will arrive 
closer to midday but as impulses rotate around the low and eject 
inland the potential for cells to develop over Idaho, Eastern and 
northern WA will increase. This looks to be closer to late 
afternoon into the evening hours. Any cells through the day, rain 
or thunderstorms that produce precipitation shafts will likely 
result in gusty outflow winds of 25 to 50 mph given the high based
nature of this convection, extremely dry subcloud layers, and 
DCAPES of 500-1500 J/kg. In the most intense outflows, winds could
gust closer to 60 mph. This will be nclosely monitored through 
the day as will lightning strikes and fire starts. 

Winds will be the other major concern through the day.  Away from 
outflow boundaries, strong synoptic driven winds will develop 
across a majority of the region, especially the Western Columbia 
Basin and through the Cascade Gaps. Winds will initially 
strengthen from the south then shift to the southwest and west 
late in the day into the evening as cooler air floods inland. Any 
ongoing or new fires will stand a good chance to be fanned by 
gusty winds of 25-35 mph. Given our fuel dryness levels, this is 
very concerning. 

Red Flag Warnings are in place across the region to account for 
the synoptic winds, outflow winds, and lightning starts. 
Generally speaking, the Cascades, Northern Mountains, and Idaho 
Panhandle are in fire weather highlights for the lightning starts 
and gusty outflow winds though the Cascades will experience a 
period of strong synoptic winds Saturday evening as the cooler air
floods into the region. This will draw higher humidity levels but
it will take several hours for the fuels to react. 

We expect very little lightning in the Western and Southern 
Columbia Basin so this will mainly be a wind and low humidity 
issue. For the eastern Basin, the combination of periods of gusty 
winds and isolated thunderstorms in the late afternoon and evening
hour makes this a dual threat for fire weather.

We will also need to watch for blowing dust on Saturday around 
Moses Lake, Ritzville, and Wilbur with a lower threat for Omak 
than previously thought. The gusty winds could also lead to 
blowing ash near any fire scars. 

The threat for showers and thunderstorms will continue well into 
the evening and overnight hours while winds remain elevated 
region-wide. The main threat for thunderstorms on Sunday will be 
in the morning with the system departing to the east and breezy 
winds becoming the most impactful weather through the day while 
temperatures cool back into the 80s.

Monday through Friday: Ensembles continue to advertise a 
progressive weather pattern next week. High pressure moves in 
Monday and Tuesday promoting a warming and drying trend. This is 
quickly interrupted by another shortwave Wednesday. The exact 
depth and track of this through the NW comes with some uncertainty
but pattern recognition would suggest another bout of windy 
conditions and possibly some thunderstorms. The pattern repeats 
itself again Thursday and Friday with the next system Friday into 
Saturday. We are not seeing a lot of signs for appreciable 
rainfall with these systems indicating fire weather concerns will 
remain elevated or higher as we navigate the end of August. /sb
